# First Read: Prosperity, opening pages 1–3 (Audition A and Audition B)

Who I read as: a 16-year-old who got this as homework, opened it the night before, and expected it to be bad. I know comics. I'm watching for anything that feels AI-made.

**Order:** I read A first, then B. So B wasn't a cold read. The robot dog falling apart in mid-air surprised me once, in A. By B I knew it was coming. Keep that in mind on everything I say about B's page 1.

---

## VERSION A

### Pulled me forward
- **A, p1, panels 3–4.** The dog walks off the dock into nothing, then falls apart in mid-air. *KLAK.* For half a second I thought I was watching a robot dog kill itself. That got me. It's the best moment in A, and it has no words.
- **A, p2, panel 3.** The old man just says "Watch." He's calm and not explaining anything. I wanted to know what he knew.
- **A, p3, panel 4.** The head clamps onto the bottom of the barge and the amber eye lights up. *clk.* It's quiet and creepy and cool, and it was a good image to stop on.
- "He stole it first." Wait, the old guy stole a lake? That's the first time I thought the story might be more than "bad guys steal water."

### I slowed down / skimmed
- I didn't skim anything. There's barely anything to skim. Three pages went by in about forty seconds.
- **A, p3, panels 1–3.** The thieves' talk slowed me down. It wasn't boring. I just had to stop and work it out (see "Lines I read twice").

### I was confused
- **A, p2, panel 1.** "They're taking it." Taking what? The dog? The barge? I worked out it meant the water from the hoses on p1. That was confused but intrigued, not lost.
- **A, p2, panels 1–2.** Who is this girl to him? She calls him "Alex," so I assumed she's not family. Maybe she works for him, or she's a neighbour. Nothing on the page tells me she's his granddaughter. I didn't know that until B.
- **A, p2, panel 4 vs p1, panel 4.** On p1 the dog splits into head, torso and legs. On p2 only the head and legs go into the water. Where did the torso go? I flipped back to check.
- **A, p3, panel 2.** "Nobody stops us." Is that a brag, or is he nervous that nobody's coming? I couldn't tell how to hear it.
- **A, p3.** Which thief is which? I lost track of who was asking and who was answering.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First seen | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| "Keel" | A p1 caption, "Keel. 2099." | No. A town? A lake? A company? I guessed it was the lake's name. |
| TJ (the dog's name) | never said | **No.** A never tells me the dog has a name. |
| Alex | A p2 p2, the girl says it | Yes, his name. No, not who he is. |
| The girl | A p2 | No name, and no relationship to Alex. |
| Why the water is worth stealing | throughout | No. I assume the water is rare, but the page never says so. |
| "He stole it first" (stole what, from whom, how) | A p3 p3 | No. It's a hook, but it's left hanging. |
| The amber eye ring | A p1 p2, again p3 p4 | No. It looks important and I don't know why. |

### Lines I read twice
- "Made it fair, you think?" Who's asking? Made *what* fair? I read it twice and I'm still not sure.
- "Nobody gets a lake fair. He stole it first." Second read, I got it: Alex stole the lake, so they're stealing it back. On first read it was a riddle.
- "Nobody stops us." I wasn't sure of the tone.
- "He's got enough." That one was fine once I read the next line.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Alex and the girl: easy. Old guy, teen girl.
- The dog: easy, but I don't know his name.
- **Thief 1 and Thief 2: couldn't tell them apart at all.** Same gear, no names. To me they're one person talking to himself.

### I felt something
- A small jolt at the dog dropping into the dark. Then relief, sort of, when it turned out the dog was doing this on purpose.
- When Alex says "Watch," I trusted him a bit.
- I felt nothing for the girl. She grabs a wrench, gets stopped, and that's all she does.

### I predicted
- The dog sabotages the barge or tracks it home.
- Alex has done this before.
- Alex really did steal the lake somehow, and the book will make me decide whose side I'm on.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
An old man and his robot dog are defending a lake that other people say he stole.

### Where I would have put it down
I wouldn't put it down in these three pages. It's too short and too strange to drop. If I wobbled, it would be **A, p3, panel 3**, the thieves' riddle talk. One more page of two anonymous guys trading half-sentences and I'd be on my phone.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
I'd turn the page. I wouldn't *need* to. The eye glowing under the hull is a great image, but nothing's at stake yet. The dog isn't in danger. The barge just has something stuck to it. I want to see what the dog does. I'm curious, not worried. And I couldn't tell you the names of anyone in it except "Alex."

---

## VERSION B

*(This was my second read. The dog-splitting surprise was already spent.)*

### Pulled me forward
- **B, p1, panel 2.** "Is TJ broken?" / "Not usually." I actually laughed. It gives me the dog's name, and it made me like the old man. That was the moment B got me.
- **B, p2, panel 2.** "That's Phantum's lake." / "It's a lake." / "It's clean." Those three short lines finally told me why anyone would steal this water: clean water is rare. A never told me that.
- **B, p3, panel 1.** "Something's under us." That's simple and it builds tension. I knew what it was and they didn't, which was fun.
- **B, p3, panel 3.** Alex stops her from calling the wardens. Why doesn't he want the cops? That made me suspicious of him, and that pulled me forward more than anything the thieves said.
- **B, p3, panel 4.** The shutters close around TJ's head. Now I'm worried about the dog.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **B, p2, panel 1, and B, p3, panel 1.** I skimmed the thieves' work chatter: "Lower the pull." "We're already late." "Pressure's good." It sounds like technician filler and I read past it.
- B has more talking overall. Page 1 had a back-and-forth in nearly every panel, and I started reading faster to get to the dog.

### I was confused
- **B, p1, panel 3.** The far shore has dry channels and empty basins, but the lake is full. Am I supposed to notice that? If I did, I wouldn't know what it means. Is someone else's land dry? I'd probably miss it entirely.
- **B, p1, panel 4.** "Let's see what they came to take." Didn't they come to take the water? Is it something else? Confused but intrigued, sort of.
- **B, p3, panels 3–4.** "Let TJ show us where it goes." So the plan is tracking? Then TJ's head gets jammed in the shutters. Is that part of the plan, or is he being crushed? I honestly couldn't tell, and I wanted to.
- "We're already late." Late for what? For whom? It's never picked up.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First seen | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Lake Keel / 2099 | only in the issue header | If that header isn't printed in the comic, I never learn the place or the year in B. Nothing inside the panels says it. |
| TJ | B p1 p2 | Yes, right away. |
| "Grandpa" / Alex | B p1 p1 | I know he's her grandpa. I never hear "Alex" said on these pages. I'd only know him as Grandpa and "Phantum." |
| "Phantum" | B p2 p2 | I guessed it's Alex's last name. That seems right, but it isn't confirmed. |
| Nera and Voss | never spoken | No. I wouldn't know those names. But I could tell them apart anyway (see below). |
| Lake wardens | B p3 p3 | Partly. Some kind of authority exists, and Alex doesn't want them. |
| Why clean water is rare | B p2 p2 | Hinted ("It's clean"). Enough for now. |
| "He stole it first" | B p2 p4 | No, same as A. |

### Lines I read twice
- "Then he stole it first." The "Then" threw me. Then *what*? It reads like a reply to a line that isn't there.
- "Let's see what they came to take." Is it a hint or just a line? I read it twice.
- "Nobody gets water that clean by being polite." That was fine on first read. Clearer than anything the thieves say in A.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Grandpa, the girl and TJ: easy.
- **The thieves: I could tell them apart.** Red hood vs. lamp helmet. One works, one watches and worries. I didn't know their names, but I knew which was which, which I never managed in A.
- The girl still doesn't have a name. She has more lines in B, but most of them ask questions for my benefit.

### I felt something
- I liked Grandpa because of "Not usually."
- I worried about TJ on the last panel. That's the first time in either version I felt anything for the dog beyond "cool robot."
- A small itch of distrust when Alex won't call the wardens. That was a good feeling to have.
- The girl irritated me a little. She's 15 and lives with this dog, and she asks "Is TJ broken?" She also says "That's not a fishing boat." Those feel like lines written so I get told things, not things she'd actually say. That's the closest either version came to feeling generated.

### I predicted
- TJ gets out of the shutters, rides the water back to wherever it's going, and Alex finds out who's behind it.
- Alex has a reason for avoiding the wardens that makes him look worse.
- "He stole it first" will turn out to be at least partly true.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A grandfather who may have done something shady to get his clean lake uses his robot dog to track down the people stealing it.

### Where I would have put it down
Not in these pages. The closest was **B, p2, panel 1**, "Lower the pull" / "We're already late," where it turned into work talk from two people I didn't know. "Something's under us" pulled me back.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Yes. I'd turn the page right now. It's a real cliffhanger: the shutters are closing on the dog I just started liking, and I don't know if it's part of the plan. That's a question about someone I care about, not just a loud noise. The one weak spot: if it turns out TJ was always fine, I'll feel tricked.

---

## Which one I would keep reading, and the moment that decided it
**B.** It was decided on **B, p1, panel 2**, "Is TJ broken?" / "Not usually.", and sealed on **B, p3, panel 4**, when the shutters close on TJ. In B I knew who everyone was, I could tell the thieves apart, I understood why the water mattered, and the last page put someone I liked in danger.

To be fair to A: A's silent drop on p1 hit harder than anything in B, and B only lost that surprise because I read A first. A felt cooler and more confident. It also felt more like a puzzle I'd have to do as homework. B felt clearer but chattier, and the girl's lines sometimes sound like they're explaining things to me. Both versions use "he stole it first," and in both it's the best hook and the least explained line.

## One-sentence aftertaste of each
- **A:** It was a cool, silent trailer where I never learned the dog's name or which thief was talking.
- **B:** It was a clearer, chattier opening that made me like the dog just in time to be scared for it.

# Cold Read — Prosperity

I read it the way the reader file describes: 16, assigned, the night before, wanting it to be bad. I read it straight through once, in order, then went back to check page numbers. Everything below is what happened on the first pass.

---

## Issue 00 — Lake Keel, 2099 (pages 1–10)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 1, panel 2.** The robot dog's head, body and legs come apart in midair and keep going. That got me. It's a strange, specific image and I wanted to see what it did next.
- **Page 1, panel 4 / page 2.** The granddaughter says "They're stealing from us" and then we cut to the thieves, who think *Alex* is the thief ("Nobody gets water that clean by being polite." / "Then he stole it first."). Two sides calling each other thieves on page 2 is a hook. I didn't know who to believe, and I liked that.
- **Pages 3–5.** TJ jamming the siphon is easy to follow. Pieces go in, the pump bucks, a leg falls off (*TINK*), the siphon collapses. Clean action, no reading needed.
- **Page 7, panel 2.** "They say you made water pay for it." This is the best line in the issue. It makes the old man someone with a past, maybe a bad one. I turned the page for that.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Pages 8–10.** Once the barge is gone, nothing happens. Alex puts a part next to a terminal, a leg gets clicked back on, lights glow, dawn comes. I skimmed page 9 completely. Panels 2–4 have no words and I didn't know what I was meant to look at.
- **Page 10.** A full-page dawn after three pages of winding down. It felt like an ending before I'd been given a story.

### I was confused
- Why doesn't Alex do anything? He stops her calling the wardens, says "Let him show us where it goes," and then... TJ comes back with a part and that's it. "Show us where it goes" never pays off. Where did it go?
- **Page 7, panel 4 / page 8.** The part's amber light blinks and "Alex notices but does not explain it." So I noticed it too and got nothing. Then he leaves it by a records terminal. I don't know why that matters.
- **Page 10.** "Find out who gets to decide what water is worth." He's an old man who owns a lake. Hasn't he already found out? Is he starting something new at 90? I couldn't tell whether this was the start of a story or the end of one.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First page | Did I ever find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Lake Keel / "the old Keel mine" | 1 | Partly. Keel turns out to be the mining town in Issue 01. I never learn how a dry, debt-ridden mine becomes this lake. |
| TJ | 1 | No. He never appears again. Nobody builds him or mentions him. |
| Nera and Voss | 2 | No. They never come back. |
| "Phantum" | 2 | Yes, it's Alex's surname (page 12). |
| The wardens | 3 | No. |
| The "commercial mark" on the part | 7 | No. Whose mark? Never said. |
| The granddaughter (who's her parent? Ada?) | 1 | No. |

### Lines I read twice
- "He knows the difference between stuck and working." (p4) Fine on the second read, but it sounds like a fortune cookie.
- "The work keeps accounts." (p7) Read it three times. Still don't know what it means as an answer to "Did you make them pay?" It reads like he's dodging, and I think I'm supposed to find that wise.
- "We know what they took. We know what they left." (p8)
- "He'll need a new part." / "So will the lake." (p9) I get that it's a parallel. I don't know what the lake's "new part" is.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Alex, the granddaughter and TJ are all clear. She asks the questions, he gives the riddles, TJ does the work.
- Nera and Voss: one has a red hood, one has a lamp helmet. That's all. Nera seems to have a conscience ("Lower the pull") but I couldn't have told you more.

### I felt something
- A little, when TJ loses the leg and the granddaughter keeps trying to click it back on (p9, panel 1). That small moment worked better than the speeches.

### I predicted
- That the book would come back to 2099 and tell me whether Alex really "made water pay." (It doesn't.)
- That Nera would turn out to be someone important. (She doesn't come back.)

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
An old man owns the only clean lake around, people say he got it dirty, and his granddaughter wants to know the truth.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 9. The action's over and three silent panels of lights and terminals gave me nothing to hold onto.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Barely. The dawn image is pretty, but "find out who decides what water is worth" is a thesis statement, not a cliffhanger. What actually pulls me on is page 7's "They say you made water pay for it." I want to know if he's a villain. That's a question about a person, and it's real. The last page just isn't where it is.

VERDICT Issue 00: put down: page 9; next issue: yes

---

## Issue 01 — The Inheritance (pages 11–22)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 12.** This is the moment the book got me for real. Seventeenth birthday, and the band reads `DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS`, `PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS`. "Happy birthday, Phantum." / "Twenty-eight point seven." Inheriting your missing dad's debt on your birthday is something I understood instantly and felt. That number did more than all of Issue 00.
- **Page 13, panel 4.** "I'm your friend, Alex. Not your exit plan." Good line. Ada was a person right away.
- **Page 16.** Hidden room behind a bookcase. It's the oldest trick there is and I still liked it. "That's one way to hide a room." / "Badly, eventually." made me smile.
- **Page 18.** Bi11bot. "Well. That took longer than expected." / "Adrian's jaw. His poorer timing." / "B11 is acceptable if the room is on fire." He's the first character with real personality. I was happy whenever he talked.
- **Page 19.** Adrian's message is short and doesn't make excuses: "I borrowed too much. I gambled some of it. I hurt you and Grandmother." Then "Question everything. Especially me." Good. That made me trust the book a bit more.
- **Page 20.** The door locks and the band goes amber. Now there's a threat.
- **Page 22.** Someone in a control room tracks the signal. Classic, but it works.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 14.** The photo and watch conversation. "Keel says he gambled." / "Grandmother says he worked." / "Those aren't opposites." / "What if both stories are incomplete?" Four panels of characters telling each other the theme. I skimmed the last two.
- **Page 17.** Equation, brass plate, map with ink ticks, pipe symbol, empty recess. That's a lot of clue-objects in one page and I didn't know which ones I was supposed to remember. I remembered none until they came back.

### I was confused
- **Page 12, panel 4.** "Behind it, the Last Chance bar is closed and dust-covered." Why am I seeing a bar? Does it matter? It never comes back.
- **Page 15.** Who is Pilar Veyra? She shows up checking a "paper dose grid" with no introduction. Later Ada turns out to be a Veyra too. Is Pilar Ada's grandmother? Aunt? A nurse? I never found out.
- **Page 15, panel 1.** Grandmother calls him "Adrian" and corrects herself. I took it as memory loss, and that landed. But "dose grid" and medicine go by fast, and I didn't know she was sick until page 23.
- **Page 18, panel 1.** "Inserts the old connector beside the empty recess." What connector? Where did it come from?
- **Page 20.** "It knows your band stopped reporting." Why did it stop? Because he went into the hidden room? Because the bot woke up? I filled it in myself, but I wasn't sure.
- **Page 21.** "Three safeguards. The first is below Site 6." / "It measures." This is where the plan gets set up and it goes by in two balloons. Three safeguards against *what*? What happens when you have all three? I went into Issue 02 not knowing what the goal was. I knew "go to the mine," not why.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First page | Did I ever find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Foreman-7 (the "-7" sounds like a robot; the art says human) | 12 | No. Never explained why a human has a number. |
| The Last Chance bar | 12 | No. |
| Pilar Veyra | 15 | Partly: she handles Grandmother's medicine. Not who she is to Ada. |
| The balanced water-drop mark | 17 | Sort of. It's Adrian's sign. |
| Alpha | 20 | One line: "routes water, assigns work and records permission." It was enough to keep going, but thin for something the whole book hangs on. |
| Halyard, Oasis | 20 | Yes, eventually. They're places further up. |
| The infrastructure spine | 20 | Roughly. |
| Safeguards | 21 | Partly. I learn what each one *is* when we find it, never what the three together are *for* until the very end. |
| Site 6 | 21 | It's a mine site. Fine. |
| Mera | 22 | Not until Issue 04. |
| "Legacy protocol" | 22 | I assumed it means Bi11bot. Never confirmed. |

### Lines I read twice
- "I saved enough for one." / "There are two mugs." / "I'm generous with containers." (p13) Took me two reads to realise she's sharing one drink between two mugs. Cute once I got it.
- "Keel's not a sentence." (p13) Sentence as in prison. Got it on the second read.
- "Those aren't opposites." (p14)
- "It is when someone has been counting for you." (p21) Read twice. I think it means "if someone's been lying to you about the numbers." It only clicked in Issue 02.
- "Not everything has to be yours because it started with your father." (p21) Fine, just heavy.
- "Then the wrongness travels efficiently." (p20) Liked it on the second read.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, Grandmother: all clear.
- Foreman-7: clear as "the guy at the checkpoint."
- Pilar: a name with a clipboard.
- Mera: a woman with a glass of water. The water-glass straightening was odd. I didn't know if it meant anything.

### I felt something
- Page 12, the debt number on his birthday.
- Page 15, Grandmother calling him by his dad's name.
- Page 19, "I hurt you and Grandmother." That was more honest than I expected.

### I predicted
- Adrian is alive somewhere.
- Mera is the villain.
- Bi11bot will turn out to have been Adrian's partner in something big.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A kid stuck with his missing dad's huge debt finds his dad's robot and a plan to expose a computer system that's cheating his town.

### Where I would have put it down
Nowhere. This issue kept me.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Yes. Someone powerful is tracking them toward the mine, and I care about Alex and Ada by now. It's a real cliffhanger, small but honest. I'd go straight on.

VERDICT Issue 01: put down: none; next issue: yes

---

## Issue 02 — The Price of Departure (pages 23–37)

### Pulled me forward

## Issue 06 — The Fourth Choice (pages 57–64)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 58, panel 4.** Alex looks from the debt number to the cloudy water and says "Easy for who?" That was a good character moment, and it echoes Lina on page 44.
- **Page 62.** The Caldera rep tries to fudge the numbers right away and Tomas catches him with a physical gauge: "You counted the pipe after you stopped counting the homes." I liked that the new system gets tested immediately, and that Tomas is the one who catches it. Easily the best page of the issue.
- **Page 63, panel 3.** The 40-credit Tomas note finally pays off. "Took you long enough." / "You kept counting." I smiled. I also finally understood page 23, sixty pages late.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 59.** Three panels, three objects, three matching sentences: "It shows what's happening. It doesn't choose what matters." / "It shows who did the work. It doesn't erase a contract." / "It shows what we promise. It doesn't make anyone obey." It's a speech built like a school essay. This is the page where the "is this AI-made?" alarm went off for me and the people I'd be reading with: same rhythm three times, every line a slogan.
- **Page 60.** More procedure: reviewers, baselines, records. I skimmed.
- **Page 61.** Four display panels in a row. `EMERGENCY AUTHORITY: RESCINDED.` `ALPHA FUNCTIONS RETAINED...` `EXISTING ALLOCATIONS... UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS.` The climax of the book happens on a screen in all caps. I didn't feel a thing. I skimmed all four.

### I was confused
- **The title says "The Fourth Choice."** What were the first three? Take power, sell to Lock, run away? I worked out a guess. The book never says.
- **Page 57.** How did all three cities end up in one hall? Who called the meeting?
- **Page 60, panel 4.** `RECIPROCAL OBLIGATION ACCEPTED.` Accepted by whom? Alpha? So the computer agrees to give up power because Alex gave a speech? I thought the whole point was that people couldn't override it.
- **Page 63, panel 2.** The debt drops from 418,107 to 314,159. Where did 104,000 credits come from? The purifier paid 12 credits a unit. I guess a lot of units sold? Nobody says. (Also, 314,159 is pi. I noticed, and then wondered if the number was a joke rather than a real amount. It pulled me out.)
- **Pages 1–10 vs. 57–64.** The book never goes back to 2099. I still don't know how Keel becomes that big clean lake, who the granddaughter is, who TJ is, who Nera and Voss work for, or whether Alex "made water pay for it." Issue 00 asked me a question and the book forgot it. And now old Alex's line, "Find out who gets to decide what water is worth," doesn't fit either. By the end he *has* decided that: the affected people decide. So why is he still asking 70 years later? Did the system fail? I genuinely can't tell if that's supposed to be sad.
- **Grandmother's cloth (p64).** I only half remembered the cloth from page 15. Her setting it down is clearly supposed to mean something. I didn't know what.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First page | Did I ever find out? |
|---|---|---|
| "Designated human authority" | 57 | Roughly. |
| Keel / Halyard / Oasis representatives | 57 | Faces I've never seen. |
| "Reciprocal obligation" | 60 | No. |
| "Revised denominator" | 62 | I worked it out from the next panel. |
| The fourth choice | title | No. |

### Lines I read twice
- "The revised denominator confirms improved delivery." (p62) Twice, then I let page 62 panel 2 explain it.
- "It doesn't erase a contract." (p59) Which contract? Lock's? The worker's? Adrian's debt?
- "We revise it in public." (p60)
- "I'm showing up." (p64) Not hard, but I paused. "You're staying?" / "I'm showing up." I like it, but it's one more line built to be quoted.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Alex, Ada, Tomas, Mera: clear.
- The representatives: interchangeable. The Caldera rep is the only one who does anything, and he only exists to be caught.
- Lina, Suri, Jalen and Ren don't really come back, except as painted names above a shop door.
- Bi11bot barely appears in the finale, and I missed him.

### I felt something
- Page 62, Tomas and the gauge. Satisfying.
- Page 64, panel 1. The pump from page 11 still running under his bracket. I noticed the callback and it was nice.
- I didn't feel the "win." Emergency authority gets rescinded on a screen and I just watched words change colour.

### I predicted
- That Adrian would turn up. (He doesn't.)
- That the book would cut back to old Alex and the granddaughter. (It doesn't.)

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
Not taking power when you could is the only way to fix a system that crushed your family, and fairness means doing the boring public paperwork forever.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 61. Four screens of all-caps system messages for the climax.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
If there were a second book: no. The last image of Alex and Ada above the town is fine, and "I'm showing up" is a real ending. But the loose threads I actually cared about were the 2099 opening (TJ, the thieves, "They say you made water pay for it") and Adrian's fate, and this page touches neither. So it doesn't make me want more. It makes me wonder why I was shown them.

VERDICT Issue 06: put down: page 61; next issue: no

## For the whole book

### The page that would have lost my whole class
**Issue 02, page 23.** It comes right after the best cliffhanger in the book (page 22, the tracking ring), and it's four disconnected panels with a new character (Tomas), an object we don't know ("the old key's travel token and parts advance") and two lines nobody can parse ("Who carries the downside?", "Make it real."). That's where half the room checks their phone and doesn't come back. Runner-up: **Issue 06, page 61**, the climax told in four system displays.

### What I would tell a friend it was about
"A kid in a mining town inherits his dead-or-missing dad's massive debt on his 17th birthday, finds his dad's robot, and proves the computer running everything has been stealing the town's water. Then he gets offered the power to fix it all himself and says no. The robot's good and Ada's good. There's a cool robot dog at the start that never comes back."

### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue
- **Issue 00:** A great falling-apart robot dog and one sharp question ("did you make them pay?") that the book never answers.
- **Issue 01:** The debt on his birthday got me, and Bi11bot kept me.
- **Issue 02:** A confusing first page, then the 62%/18% pipe reveal, which is the moment the book makes sense.
- **Issue 03:** Four strangers build a filter in a montage and the issue ends on a receipt.
- **Issue 04:** Three honest pages between Ada and her mother, swallowed by a history lecture.
- **Issue 05:** "It used the same shape," and a door closing on Adrian's hand. The best the book gets.
- **Issue 06:** The right choice, made in a speech and confirmed by a screen, with the opening's questions left on the dock.

# Analysis — Prosperity, pages 1–64

I read the script cold, as the pages a student, a teacher, the partner and the backer would hold. I go by page number, and I mark it when I'm guessing beyond what the page shows ("inference").

---

## The political read

| Reading | Signal | Pages that carry it |
|---|---|---|
| **Progressive** | **Some, close to strong** | The residential pipe is "nearly dry, stained orange and white" while a "broad maintained industrial uplink" runs above it (p30). Homes are told 62% and get 18% (p32). The water comes out "cloudy and orange" (p38), which any teacher will read as Flint. A House takes a worker's invention for a 14-credit bonus (p39). The ending is public accountability: "Anyone affected can challenge the evidence" (p60). |
| **Libertarian** | **Strong** | Alpha is a central system that "routes water, assigns work and records permission" (p20). It is the machine that locks Alex in (p20, p24, p51). The emergency authority behind the whole mess is voted in (p47) and then "RESCINDED" (p61). Alex turns down executive power twice (p50, p59). Ownership records stay "UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS" (p61). The Maker's Seal records who made the thing (p44). |
| **Conservative** | **Some** | Debts get paid (p23, p35, p63). A father owns his failure: "I borrowed too much… The mistakes were mine" (p19). Family care comes first: "Medicine first" (p23). The suspicion of emergency powers (p47, p52) will read to some adults as a post-2020 cue (inference). |
| **Socialist** | **Some, leaning weak** | "Workers open ledgers… on a communal table" (p34). Neighbours pool credits (p35). Tomas says "We're already in it" (p34). Workers audit the House (p62). Against that, ownership is never taken away, and the closing commerce is a licensed shop (p63). |
| **Capitalist in a bad way** | **Some** | Caldera House takes ownership of a worker's repair (p39). Director Lock offers to clear the debt in exchange for the estate (p40). The Caldera representative cooks the denominator (p62). The book never says whether the Houses are companies or a chartered arm of Alpha, so a reader may file them under "corporations." |
| **Capitalist in a good way** | **Strong from Issue 03 on** | Tomas's 40-credit loan, "Separate from your household account… Make it real" (p23). The team fails at 11% and reaches 91%, with an honest "NOT POTABLE-OUTPUT GUARANTEE" (p42–43). The first sale splits 38 credits into debt, venture and warranty reserve (p44). A customer "agrees to the posted repair price" with the makers' names above the door (p63). Repayment is still "IN PROGRESS" (p63). |

**What the surface invites:** the first 22 pages read as a dystopia about a rigged system. The prologue's thieves say the hero "stole it first" (p2), and the granddaughter says "They say you made water pay for it" (p7). Nobody answers either line. Then "TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY" hands a 17-year-old his father's 418,607 credits (p12), and an algorithm locks his door (p20). A teacher flipping through Issue 01 alone sees debt and pricing as the villain.

**What the story supports:** the villain is central control and falsified records, not trade. The fix is accurate measurement, recorded ownership and agreements anyone can challenge. Honest business pays the debt down (p44, p63).

**Who stops because of the surface:**
- A Young Americans staff member or a Denver teacher previewing only Issue 01 sees "debt as something done to you" (p12) before Issue 03 answers it.
- A progressive teacher who reads p1–10 may take the frame as "the hero owns the water and prices it" and never reach p44.
- Students are more likely to stop for clarity than for politics (see below).

**Does the book conclude, or leave a reader concluding, that free enterprise is bad? No.** Pages 44, 61 and 63 close on licensed sale, property records left untouched, and a priced repair agreed by the customer. One loose end: "Then he stole it first" (p2) and "made water pay for it" (p7) are never answered.

---

## Young Americans Center

**What they would like:**
- Water is now on the page from panel one (p1–10), and Keel's channels and pump hall follow (p11, p13).
- Tomas's loan is set up like a real note: separate from the household account, owed in full, and still tracked at the end: "STATUS: REPAYMENT IN PROGRESS" (p23, p63).
- Alex pays for doing the right thing. Freeing Tomas costs him a wage: "−40 CR," and "You know that costs you." / "I noticed." (p24). That is integrity under pressure.
- Lock's offer to clear the debt (p40) and the executive debt clearance (p50, p58) are both refused. Nobody powerful cancels the debt.
- Issue 03 is the profit-and-IP story they asked for. The registry shows 312 patents (p39). The team fails, then iterates: "Smaller failure" (p42). The Seal records "who has to answer when it fails" (p44). The first sale splits revenue into debt, venture and warranty reserve (p44). A licensed shop sells to a customer who agrees the price (p63).
- Adrian's confession, "I borrowed too much… The mistakes were mine" (p19), is close to their founder's ethic.

**What would bother them:**
- **The credit mechanics.** They are a real bank. A debt transferred to a 17-year-old (p12) goes unexamined. The balance falls from 418,107 to 314,159 (p63), about 104,000 credits, and nothing shown on the page accounts for it. At 12 credits a unit (p44) that is roughly 8,700 purifiers, and the book doesn't say so.
- **The neighbours' 500 credits** (p35) pay his installment. Nobody says it will be repaid, and Alex's only response is "They bought the gate."
- **Who the villains are.** Caldera House reads as a company taking workers' IP (p39) and fiddling its numbers (p62). Nothing on the page marks it as a crony of Alpha rather than a business.
- **Still hard to follow in places:**
  - Ten pages of prologue with thieves who never return (p1–10).
  - Mera (p22) and Nera (p2) have nearly the same name.
  - "Tomas receives the old key's travel token and parts advance" (p23) reads backwards.
  - Riddle lines remain: "The work keeps accounts" (p7), "Badly, eventually" (p16), "Two of three. Again." (p50).
  - Pilar Veyra (p15) shares Ada's surname (p45) and is never explained.
- **The climax** (p57–61) is a civics resolution, not an enterprise one. Taking charge here means declining power, which they will respect, but it is not YouthBiz.
- **Alex never fails personally and owns it.** The team's prototype fails (p42) and Bi11bot is wrong (p25, p29). Alex is right almost every time.

**Likely verdict: partly.** This draft would clear the bar they set ("cannot ethically present"), with notes on credit accuracy and clarity (inference from their own notes).

---

## Bill Reynolds

**What he would like:**
- Adrian says nearly Bill's own sentence: "I borrowed too much. I gambled some of it." (p19).
- No windfall solves the plot. Debt clearance is refused three times (p40, p50, p58). The debt is still mostly owed at the end (p63).
- **Ownership made concrete, de Soto style.** The creator's name "vanishes from the ownership field" (p39) until the Maker's Seal writes it down (p44). After that, the work becomes income (p44, p63). This is the book's strongest match to his beliefs.
- Central control is the villain, and "EMERGENCY AUTHORITY: RESCINDED" (p61) is a libertarian ending.
- The mentor is sometimes wrong: "I predicted we could leave him unseen." / "You were wrong." / "Yes. What would you do?" (p25), and "I read that wrong." (p29). He asks more than he tells: "Who carries the downside?" (p23).
- Bi11bot does not replace people. He mostly fades out after Issue 02. The resolution belongs to Ada, Tomas and the representatives (p57–62).
- "I'm showing up" (p64) echoes "Technology… cannot replace presence."

**What would bother him:**
- The neighbours' collection (p35) is a gift Alex never answers. "We don't believe in charity" is his line.
- The unexplained debt drop (p63) can look like a quiet windfall.
- He never gets his beer-hall scene. No young person says "I can't pay you" and works out terms with the lender. Tomas's "Took you long enough" (p63) is the nearest moment, and it is one line.
- p59–61 is a young man explaining the system to a room. That is a lecture, which he says he never gives.
- "TJ," if it is his Founder dog, appears only in 2099 (p1–9). The name is never explained and the dog is absent from the main story.

**Does Bi11bot sound like him? No, only in part.** By the profile's voice notes (plain, slow, roundabout, Western, question first, then a story from his own life, then one plain line, jokes at his own expense), Bi11bot gets the questions (p23, p25) and the fallibility (p29). He gets nothing else:
- He is clipped and arch, a dry butler-robot: "Then the wrongness travels efficiently" (p20), "B11 is acceptable if the room is on fire" (p18).
- His one joke is at Adrian's expense, not his own: "Adrian's jaw. His poorer timing." (p18).
- There is no story from his own life, no Western cadence, and no "damn hard."

**Likely verdict: partly.** The beliefs are honoured, but the voice that was supposed to be his isn't.

---

## A comic writer

**The hook:** the real hook is on p12: a 17th birthday, "DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS — PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS," and "Happy birthday, Phantum." That is a strong first-issue hook, and it arrives on page twelve. The prologue (p1–10) is a nice robot-dog heist, but it belongs to an old man and two thieves who never come back. Its threads go nowhere: the blinking amber indicator (p7) and the missing leg (p9).

**Page turns:** the right/left plan is used well. The reveals land on left pages:
- p12, the debt
- p16, the bookcase
- p18, Bi11bot
- p32, the 62/18 numbers
- p50, the offer
- p54, Adrian
- p64, the final image

**Splash pages:** two are broken as written. p10 is called "FULL-PAGE IMAGE" and then given Panels 2 and 3. p57 is called "FULL-PAGE CIVIC HALL" and then given three more panels. An artist will send both back. The p64 full-width final panel works.

**Dialogue:**
- It is tight and has good moments: "I'm generous with containers" (p13), "Abandoned mines do not sweat" (p27), "You counted the pipe after you stopped counting the homes" (p62).
- But everyone speaks in the same wry two-beat line. Ada, Bi11bot, Alex, Lock and Tomas are hard to tell apart with the names covered.
- Names collide: Mera/Nera, Lina/Leona, and Ada/Adrian/Alex/Alpha.
- p44's roll call ("Lina: membrane chemistry. Suri: living biofilter…") is the writer talking, not Alex.

**What they would cut:**
- Cut p1–10 to three pages, or drop it.
- Cut p61, a page of nothing but displays.
- Fold p53 and p55 into one page.

**Would they take the job?** Yes, as a rewrite with a free hand on the prologue and the Issue 06 climax (inference). The skeleton holds: debt → Measure → build → Covenant → refusal → audit. It has a clean three-object structure and a good antagonist in Mera.

---

## A game designer

**Is there a game? Yes, and an obvious one.**

**The loop:** measure (find the gap between what's reported and what's delivered), expose (publish or route privately), build (combine contributors' parts, fail, iterate from 11% to 91%), license and sell, pay down the debt, unlock the next city.

**Choices that cost something:**
- Leave the zone to save Tomas and lose 40 credits (p24).
- The private route or the public one (p33).
- Sell the estate for debt clearance or keep it with commercial rights frozen (p40).
- Take executive authority (p50, p58).

All are real trade-offs with numbers attached.

**Systems a player would push on:**
- Can you game Alpha's allocation?
- The revenue split (p44): what happens if you cut the warranty reserve?
- The evidence-challenge mechanic (p62), which is a ready-made audit minigame.
- Contributor loyalty and compatibility (the sleeve bridging standards, p43).
- A debt meter that visibly ticks (p12, p35, p63).

**The weak spot:** the Covenant bands (p45–56) are a fetch quest with no system under them. "Two of three" is a key count, not a choice.

**Would they want to build it?** Yes. It sits close to the partner's own Young AmeriTowne simulation (inference).

---

## A streaming showrunner

**The engine:** a kid with an inherited debt, a dead-or-missing father's 312 patents (each one a locked door, so each one an episode), and a three-tier water world where the records lie. That is renewable.

**Characters an audience would follow for a season:**
- **Alex**, who needs a flaw. He is right too often.
- **Ada**, who has the best personal arc (p45–48).
- **Tomas**, a working-class wit and the series' conscience.
- **Mera**, the best character in the book: sympathetic, powerful, and once beaten by her own system. "I was the most powerful person in Oasis. I could not stop a door from closing." (p52).
- **Lock**, underused.

**Season-one cliffhanger:** Adrian behind the sealed bulkhead, "The image cuts before showing what happens beyond it" (p55). Also the 2099 frame: who sent the thieves, and what did the blinking component mean (p7)?

**What's missing:**
- A face for the threat in episode one. Mera gets two panels (p22).
- Personal stakes beyond a number.
- Any romance or friction between Alex and Ada.
- The p1–10 frame tells the audience Alex lives and wins a lake, which drains suspense.
- The finale is a public hearing (p57–62). That plays as a bottle episode, not a season ender.

**Would they see a series in the first issue?** Probably yes, on p12–19 (debt, the hidden room, the father's hologram). They would doubt it on p1–10.

---

## Does it smell like school

**Pages that exist to explain, or state the lesson:**
1. **p31**: the Measure's collar is engraved "WHAT IS NOT MEASURED CAN BE MADE INVISIBLE." The theme is printed on a prop.
2. **p47**: Leona narrates the Covenant's founding and the vote for emergency authority. It is backstory delivered straight to the reader.
3. **p59**: a **whole page** where Alex defines each safeguard ("It shows what's happening. It doesn't choose what matters." ×3). This is the book's glossary, read aloud.
4. **p60**: Alex sets out the procedure: "The affected districts choose their reviewers… Anyone affected can challenge the evidence."
5. **p61**: a **whole page** of system displays stating the civic outcome, with no characters acting.

**Borderline, not counted:** p20–21 (Bi11bot's one-line definitions of Alpha and the safeguards, which students need), and p44 panel 1 (the contributor roll call).

**Count: 5.** p59 is a whole page that exists to explain. So the book smells like school, but only in the climax, which is where a student reading the night before will judge it.

**Pages that teach without smelling of it, because people need the thing and pay for it:**
- p23 (Tomas's loan; medicine first in the budget)
- p24 (the wage forfeited for helping)
- p32 and p34 (62% vs 18%, the same thirty days)
- p35 (the installment arithmetic is exact)
- p39 (the creator bonus vs ownership)
- p42–43 (iterating, and an honest "not a guarantee")
- p44 (the revenue split and warranty reserve)
- p62 (an audit catches a doctored baseline)
- p63 (the posted price and the outstanding note)

This is the book at its best.

`EXECUTIVE CLEARANCE AVAILABLE.`

ADA: They made it look easy.

ALEX: Easy for who?

ALEX: It shows what’s happening. It doesn’t choose what matters.

**Panel 2.** He places the Maker’s Seal beside the contributor records.

ALEX: It shows who did the work. It doesn’t erase a contract.

ALEX: It shows what we promise. It doesn’t make anyone obey.

ALEX: No executive designation.

## Page 60 (left) — The room must accept an obligation before Alpha can change its authority.

ALEX: No one approves an allocation alone. The affected districts choose their reviewers.

ALEX: We publish the measurements, name the contributors and record every decision. Anyone affected can challenge the evidence.

**Panel 4.** Mera places her hand beside the bands.

MERA: And if the record is false?

ALEX: We revise it in public.

DISPLAY: `RECIPROCAL OBLIGATION ACCEPTED.`

`EMERGENCY AUTHORITY: RESCINDED.`

**Panel 2.** Across the hall, white-and-amber nodes shift from command amber to steady white.

**Panel 3.** A second display reads:

`ALPHA FUNCTIONS RETAINED:`  
`MEASUREMENT — ROUTING — PAYROLL — MAINTENANCE — RECORD PUBLICATION`

**Panel 4.** The final display reads:

`EXISTING ALLOCATIONS, OWNERSHIP RECORDS AND AGREEMENTS: UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS.`

## Page 62 (left) — The first public review is tested by a changed denominator.

**Panel 1.** A Caldera representative submits a polished allocation proposal.

CALDERA REPRESENTATIVE: The revised denominator confirms improved delivery.

**Panel 2.** The public display reveals that the baseline excludes the old residential branch.

**Panel 3.** Tomas places a physical gauge beside the proposal.

TOMAS: You counted the pipe after you stopped counting the homes.

**Panel 4.** Keel workers compare the gauge, the Measure’s baseline and the House proposal.

DISPLAY: `EVIDENCE CHALLENGE FILED.`

PAGE CHECK: People use the new process to challenge an actual decision.

---

## Page 63 (right) — Keel forces revision, and Alex’s debt falls through visible work.

**Panel 1.** The Caldera representative revises the proposal while the public record updates.

DISPLAY: `PROPOSAL REVISED — RESIDENTIAL BRANCH INCLUDED.`

**Panel 2.** Alex’s account displays:

`HOUSEHOLD DEBT BALANCE: 314,159 CREDITS.`  
`VISIBLE PAYMENTS: INSTALLMENT — WAGES — REPAIRS — PURIFIER ALLOCATION`

**Panel 3.** A separate receipt reads:

`TOMAS NOTE: 40 CREDITS — KEY / TRAVEL TOKEN / PARTS`  
`STATUS: REPAYMENT IN PROGRESS`

TOMAS: Took you long enough.

ALEX: You kept counting.

**Panel 4.** In Keel, a licensed shop services a purifier. A customer counts credits and agrees to the posted repair price. The contributors’ names are painted above the door.

PAGE CHECK: The fixed balance comes through visible repayments. Tomas’s note remains separate.

---

## Page 64 (left) — Alex returns to Keel and chooses to remain answerable.

**Panel 1.** The old Keel pump runs beneath Alex’s repaired bracket. Water moves through the channel, still imperfect but measured.

SFX: THRUM

**Panel 2.** Public records remain open on a wall display. Workers study the figures while Tomas argues with a House representative nearby.

**Panel 3.** In Grandmother’s apartment, Pilar closes the paper dose ledger. Grandmother sets down the cloth she has folded throughout the book.

**Panel 4 — FULL-WIDTH FINAL IMAGE.** Alex and Ada stand above Keel. Pipes, rails, lights and control nodes climb toward Halyard and Oasis beneath the mountain sky.

ADA: You’re staying?

ALEX: I’m showing up.

PAGE CHECK: The final question belongs to Alex and Ada. The system is visible, imperfect and still dependent on people who keep showing up.

# Note from the showrunner — address this first

The room is in writing: The writer you picked writes the whole script.

The showrunner picked you in the audition. script.md holds your audition pages: keep their voice, and write the whole book.

Drawability: Pages are drawn by an image model, one page per generation, from each character's and location's sheet, and a page drifts when it carries too much. So: at most 4 panels a page; at most 3 named characters in one panel; one location a page where the story allows (every new location needs its own sheet); no crowd that must be recognisable; a big moment gets a splash (one panel, the whole page). Count pages this way, not by comic convention. Every page you make keeps to it.

The book is exactly 64 pages: pages 1-64, no more, no fewer.

Showrunner's note for this round: This revision is a CUT PASS. The Analyst has read the whole script, the pages only, as the book's partner (Young Americans Center), its backer (Bill Reynolds) and three professionals would; the report is analysis.md. Its "Does it smell like school" section numbers every page where a line or caption exists to teach. Take each one in turn: cut the line, or replace it with something a person does, wants or pays for on the page. A lesson replaced by another lesson is not a fix. Then make the report's "What would change the verdicts" changes the same way: through what happens, never through what someone says about it. The cold readers are not all won: cold-read.md: does not want the issue after Issue 03; cold-read-b.md: does not want the issue after Issue 03. Fix those pages too (cold-read.md, cold-read-b.md): a first page that loses a reader is a page that explains, and a last page nobody wants to turn is not yet a question about a person. The script is 6504 words. It comes back no longer than that. Say in notes.md what you cut, page by page.

# Prosperity — Script

## Chapter 00 — Lake Keel, 2099

## Page 1 (right) — Older Alex sees water being stolen from the restored lake.

**Panel 1.** NIGHT. The old Keel mine is now a lake ringed by terraces, gardens and workshops. Drones lower siphons from a tanker barge.

GRANDDAUGHTER: Grandpa. That’s not a fishing boat.

ALEX: No.

**Panel 2.** TJ, a small lopsided magnetic robot dog, springs from the dock. His head, body and legs separate in midair.

SFX: KLAK-KLAK-KLAK

GRANDDAUGHTER: Is TJ broken?

ALEX: Not usually.

**Panel 3.** TJ’s pieces skim toward the barge. The siphon lifts a bright column of water. Dry channels scar the far shore.

**Panel 4.** A drone beam sweeps the dock. The granddaughter catches Alex’s sleeve.

GRANDDAUGHTER: They’re stealing from us.

ALEX: Let’s see what they came to take.

PAGE CHECK: The future is restored but contested.

---

## Page 2 (left) — The thieves reveal that the lake’s history is disputed.

**Panel 1.** On the tanker barge, Nera in a red hood checks the siphon. Voss, in a lamp helmet, watches the shore.

NERA: Lower the pull.

VOSS: We’re late.

**Panel 2.** Voss studies the distant boathouse. The tanker gauge rises.

VOSS: That’s Phantum’s lake.

NERA: It’s a lake.

VOSS: It’s clean.

**Panel 3.** TJ’s head glides beneath the barge. A magnetic leg hooks a submerged brace.

SFX: TIK

**Panel 4.**

VOSS: Nobody gets water that clean by being polite.

NERA: Then he took it first.

PAGE CHECK: Both sides call the other thief.

---

## Page 3 (right) — Alex chooses evidence over an immediate attack.

**Panel 1.** Nera tightens the coupling. Voss sees movement beneath the rail.

NERA: Pressure’s good.

VOSS: Something’s under us.

**Panel 2.** TJ’s head catches the siphon housing.

SFX: GRRNNNK

**Panel 3.** The granddaughter reaches for an emergency radio. Alex stops her.

GRANDDAUGHTER: We can call the wardens.

ALEX: After the water’s gone.

**Panel 4.** Rotating shutters close around TJ’s head.

ALEX: Let him show us where it goes.

PAGE CHECK: TJ is in danger; investigation becomes the choice.

---

## Page 4 (left) — TJ sabotages the siphon.

**Panel 1.** TJ’s head strains between the shutters. His legs reach through a maintenance gap.

SFX: KRRRNNK

**Panel 2.** Nera opens the service panel. A magnetic leg snaps onto the inner latch.

NERA: Something’s in the housing.

VOSS: Shut it down.

**Panel 3.** The siphon bucks. Water sprays across the deck.

SFX: WHUMP—KRAK

**Panel 4.** On the dock, the granddaughter grips the rail.

GRANDDAUGHTER: He’s stuck.

ALEX: He’s working.

PAGE CHECK: Action carries TJ’s purpose.

---

## Page 5 (right) — The theft fails, but TJ loses a piece.

**Panel 1.** TJ wedges the pump rotor. One leg tears free and drops into the lake.

SFX: TINK

**Panel 2.** Voss swings a work lamp toward the water. Nera sees TJ’s amber lens.

NERA: That’s not driftwood.

VOSS: Pull him out.

**Panel 3.** The siphon collapses. A reduced stream pours back into the lake.

SFX: FWOOOSH

**Panel 4.** TJ’s head sinks briefly. His remaining pieces move toward it.

PAGE CHECK: The theft is interrupted, not defeated.

---

## Page 6 (left) — TJ returns with evidence.

**Panel 1.** Underwater, TJ’s lens catches a broken drone component.

**Panel 2.** His body and remaining legs converge. One leg clamps onto the component.

SFX: CLK

**Panel 3.** The tanker retreats with less water than planned.

VOSS: Move!

NERA: I’m moving.

**Panel 4.** TJ reaches the dock dragging the component.

GRANDDAUGHTER: He brought something.

ALEX: He usually does.

PAGE CHECK: The theft leaves physical evidence.

---

## Page 7 (right) — The granddaughter asks how Alex came to own the lake.

**Panel 1.** Alex fits TJ’s body together. One leg is missing.

GRANDDAUGHTER: How did you get this lake?

ALEX: I didn’t.

**Panel 2.** She holds the damaged drone component.

GRANDDAUGHTER: They say you made water pay for it.

**Panel 3.** The barge disappears across the lake.

GRANDDAUGHTER: Did you make them pay?

Alex studies the component.

**Panel 4.** The component’s amber indicator blinks beside an open public water terminal.

---

## Page 8 (left) — Alex refuses to chase the thieves.

GRANDDAUGHTER: We can catch them.

ALEX: Not across open water.

GRANDDAUGHTER: They left less than they planned.

SFX: CLICK

GRANDDAUGHTER: He’ll need a new part.

**Panel 3.** Public lights mark the lake’s gauges and channels.
